newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Can Major the survivor spring back this time?.
newsitem.headline: Can Major the survivor spring back this time?.

text.p: The betting odds are stacked against him, opinion polls give him no chance.
But British Prime Minister John Major, underestimated ever since emerging as Conservative leader mainly because he was not Margaret Thatcher, has a Houdini-like ability to survive.

At the last election, Major confounded polls to put the Conservatives back in office for a fourth term. Last year he stunned everyone by stepping down as party leader to take on and defeat the right-wingers who were crippling his leadership.
The question is, what can he pull out of the bag this time?
In the past week, he has been hit with a triple whammy.
Sleaze has reemerged with new allegations about payments from lobbyists to former trade minister Neil Hamilton.
His rival, Labour leader Tony Blair, staged a triumphal party conference which sent his 20-point-plus poll lead soaring higher and even impressed right-wing newspapers.
And finally, Major's attempts to survive Saturday's European summit without controversy were sabotaged by a bitter attack from the European Parliament president, socialist Klaus Haensch.

Major, already angry with Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and Portuguese premier Antonio Guterres -- all socialists -- for endorsing Blair in videos made for the Labour conference, was furious.

He battled back, berating Haensch publicly, upbraiding Vranitzky, Guterres and Kok, dismissing allegations of a cover- up over Hamilton and laying down to other European leaders his standard line over Europe, "Look before you leap".
But as preparation for next week's Conservative party conference, the jumping off point for the general election now no more than seven months away, it could not have been worse.
Two polls published over the weekend illustrate the scale of the challenge facing him if he is not to preside over the end of 17 years of unbroken Conservative rule.

A Gallup poll for Saturday's Daily Telegraph said Blair's poll lead had soared to 33 points from the 24.5 he had just before his conference. And an NOP poll for the Sunday Times said Blair's lead had gone up four points to 23.
Major's problem is not so much his leadership as his party.
Voters generally consider Major to be a decent and honourable man who has done his best on intractable problems such as how to bring peace to Northern Ireland.

But they overwhelmingly see his Conservative party as corrupt and out of touch, and Major only needs to utter the word "Europe" for so-called Eurosceptics in his parliamentary party go on the warpath, followed closely by the pro-Europeans.

Marshalled against this chronically divided and unpopular party is Labour, revitalised by a charismatic leader and a team of strategists who have ruthlessly imposed discipline and ditched the socialist dogmas of the past.
Major's main hope is that an expanding economy will restore the elusive "feelgood factor" as voters' spending power grows.
Tax cuts in the next budget could ratchet up that effect.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has already made it clear he is not prepared to risk the long-term health of the economy with short-term measures for electoral gain.
This prudent advice is no comfort to Major. And some commentators see an ulterior motive behind Clarke's caution.
Clarke is battling against Eurosceptic efforts to push the ruling party to the right -- and some see him as positioning himself for a party leadership bid if Major loses the election.

Clarke is not alone. The party conference is likely to see more covert bids by colleagues to position themselves to succeed Major. To pull this one off, Major needs an escape routine not even Houdini would have been able to think up.
